## Intent
Hypothesis: fusing integrate+decide+respawn+render into a single register-only pass with no intermediate storage eliminates extra bandwidth and approaches the streaming ceiling.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout at 68 B/particle offers 48 hot bytes (70%) — age, color, pos, seed, vel — while 20 bytes are dead weight dragged through every cache line fill. The fused approach keeps the death verdict in registers (no intermediate storage), which should save a write-back pass, but the single loop must also perform the framebuffer scatter, which is byte-granular (`strb` ×19) and indexed — fundamentally unstreamable. The working set spills L1d at N≈963 and L2 at N≈61680, but since the loop body is 237 instructions per iteration, cache residency matters less than instruction throughput.

## Cache saturation
The ns/particle curve is flat across all regimes: ~7.3–7.5 ns/p at q=0.01 in L1d (N=380–960), holding ~7.0–7.6 through L2 (N=1400–41000), and even slightly improving to ~6.8–7.2 in DRAM (N≥62000). There is no cache-spill knee — the L1d→L2 transition at N≈963 and the L2→DRAM transition at N≈61680 are invisible in the cost curve. This is the signature of a compute-bound loop: memory latency is hidden behind the 237-instruction body, so adding DRAM latency changes nothing. The dense grid confirms the absence of any knee.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth peaks at ~9.9 GB/s (q=0.01, N=93000) — only 33% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling — against a memory floor of 2.274 ns/p. Actual cost of 7–7.5 ns/p is 3× the floor, confirming the algo is not bandwidth-bound but compute/branch-bound. Bandwidth degrades sharply with death rate: 9–10 GB/s at q=0.01, 8.2–8.6 at q=0.1, 6.7–7.2 at q=0.25, and 5.1–5.5 at q=0.5. The algo ties the naive scalar baseline everywhere (0.90–1.01×) and loses to the winner by 1.5–2.0× at q=0.01, widening to 2.3–2.4× at q=0.5 — the branchy respawn is the equalizer that drags both this algo and the baseline down together.

## Assembly
The codegen is overwhelmingly scalar: 9 vector instructions out of 296, with the loop body at 237 insns/iter and 24 conditional branches. The integration uses limited vectorization — `fmul.4s`, `fadd.4s`, `ext.16b`, `dup.4s` — on the position update, but the color clamp and render path are fully scalar (`fcmp`/`fcvtzs`/`csel` chains ×18). The framebuffer scatter is byte-granular: `ldrb`/`strb` pairs with indexed addressing via `mul`/`lsl`/`add`, making it impossible to stream. The death decision uses `fcmp`/`b.ge` with a `bl` call to `spawn` — a true branch, not a select. The 18 `csel` instructions show the compiler tried select-based death handling but could not eliminate the branchy respawn call. This scalar-dominated codegen with byte-granular scatter explains why achieved bandwidth stalls at 33% of ceiling.

## Verdict
Refuted — the fused single-pass approach ties the naive scalar at every point (0.90–1.01× baseline) and never approaches the winner, losing 1.5–2.0× at q=0.01 and 2.3–2.4× at q=0.5. The mechanism is clear: 237 instructions per iteration with only 9 vector instructions means the loop is compute-bound at 3× the memory floor, and the byte-granular framebuffer scatter (`strb` ×19) plus branchy respawn (branch_flush rising to 33% at q=0.5) prevent streaming regardless of the fused structure. Keeping the verdict in registers saves nothing when the render scatter dominates.
